subtopics.title: Friction: useful and harmful
subtopics.theory_md:
**Friction** is the resistance to relative motion between two surfaces in contact. It arises because the surface peaks (**asperities**) interlock and momentarily weld. Coefficient of friction $\mu = F/N$ ($F$ frictional force, $N$ normal load).

**Useful:** brakes, clutches, belt drives, walking, tyre grip, nuts and bolts.

**Harmful between moving parts:**
- **Wear** and loss of dimensions
- **Heat**, causing expansion and seizure
- **Loss of energy**, lower efficiency
- Noise and vibration
subtopics.basics_md: Rub your palms together: they get warm and the skin wears slowly. That resistance is friction. It is helpful when you want a grip and wasteful when you want a machine to spin freely.
key_points: Friction = resistance to relative motion, due to interlocking and welding of asperities
$\mu = F/N$
Useful: brakes, clutches, belts, walking, nuts and bolts
Harmful: wear, heat and seizure, energy loss, noise

questions.q: Why do two polished metal surfaces still show friction? Give three harmful effects.
questions.model_answer_md:
No surface is perfectly smooth. Under magnification it has peaks (**asperities**). When pressed together the surfaces touch only at the peaks, which interlock and may weld momentarily; shearing these junctions is friction.

Harmful effects:
1. **Wear and tear** of parts
2. **Heat** generation, leading to expansion and seizure
3. **Loss of energy**, so lower efficiency

questions.q: A dry steel block under a normal load of 300 N needs a force of 45 N to slide. After lubrication only 6 N is needed. Find $\mu$ in each case and the fall in friction.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\mu = F/N$
- Dry: $\mu = 45/300 = 0.15$
- Lubricated: $\mu = 6/300 = 0.02$
- Friction force falls by $(45-6)/45 \times 100 = 86.7\%$.

subtopics.title: Lubricant and the three regimes
subtopics.theory_md:
A **lubricant** is a substance placed between moving surfaces to reduce friction and wear; **lubrication** is the process. It replaces solid (dry) friction by the much smaller **internal friction** of the lubricant.

Schematic of the three states:
1. **Dry:** asperities interlock, high friction, wear and heat.
2. **Thin film (boundary):** a few molecules thick, some peaks touch, $\mu \approx 0.05$-$0.15$.
3. **Thick film (fluid):** film thicker than the peaks, no contact, $\mu \approx 0.001$-$0.03$.
subtopics.basics_md: Think of walking on dry ground versus on a wet floor with a thin sheet of water: the sheet takes over the job of the rough ground. A lubricant is that sheet.
key_points: Lubricant reduces friction and wear; lubrication is the process
Solid friction replaced by internal (fluid) friction of the lubricant

Thick film $\mu \approx 0.001$-$0.03$, boundary $\approx 0.05$-$0.15$

subtopics.title: Functions of a lubricant
subtopics.theory_md:
A lubricant:
1. **Reduces friction**, so less power is wasted.
2. **Reduces wear and tear**.
3. **Acts as a coolant**, carrying frictional heat away.
4. **Prevents corrosion** by keeping air and moisture off the metal.
5. **Acts as a seal**, e.g. piston rings and cylinder in an IC engine.
6. **Reduces noise**, flushes away dirt and debris, **transmits pressure** in hydraulic systems and lowers maintenance cost.

Number the points and add a few words to each.

subtopics.title: Cooling, sealing and corrosion in practice
subtopics.theory_md:
- **Coolant:** frictional heat is carried by circulating oil to the sump or radiator, so parts do not expand or seize. Water cools better but cannot lubricate, so cutting fluids combine both.
- **Seal:** a thin oil film fills the gap between piston rings and cylinder wall and stops combustion gases leaking.
- **Corrosion:** the film keeps oxygen and moisture off the metal.
- **Hydraulics:** oil transmits pressure and lubricates pumps and valves.

questions.q: Give three reasons why plain water cannot replace oil as a lubricant even though it cools well.
questions.model_answer_md:
1. **Very low viscosity**: the film is squeezed out under load and metal contact occurs.

subtopics.title: Thick film (hydrodynamic and hydrostatic)
subtopics.theory_md:
**Thick film (fluid film) lubrication:** a continuous film, at least about $1000\,\mathring{A}$ thick, thicker than the asperities, completely separates the surfaces. No metal contact; resistance is only the **viscosity** of the oil, $\mu \approx 0.001$-$0.03$. Low load, high speed. Lubricant: mineral oil of correct viscosity.

**Hydrodynamic:** the rotating shaft drags oil into the converging wedge of a journal bearing; the pressure built up lifts the shaft. Needs motion.
**Hydrostatic:** an external pump forces oil in, so the film exists even at zero speed; for heavy load, low speed, precision.
subtopics.basics_md: A water-skier is lifted by the water only once the boat is moving fast enough. That is hydrodynamic. Pumping water under the ski while standing still would be hydrostatic.

Friction only from viscosity; $\mu \approx 0.001$-$0.03$
Low load, high speed; mineral oils
Hydrodynamic: film pressure from motion (wedge), e.g. journal bearing
Hydrostatic: pressure from external pump, works at zero speed, e.g. telescope mounts

questions.q: Explain the thick layer mechanism. How does it account for hydrodynamic lubrication?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Thick layer mechanism**
- A continuous film at least about 1000 Å thick, more than the asperity height, separates the surfaces; no metal contact.
- Only the internal friction (**viscosity**) of the oil resists motion; $\mu \approx 0.001$-$0.03$.
- Low load, high speed; mineral oils.

**Hydrodynamic lubrication**
- A shaft at rest touches the bearing. On rotation it drags oil into the **converging wedge**; the pressure generated lifts the shaft onto a film.
- The film is generated by the motion itself. Example: crankshaft and turbine journal bearings.

subtopics.title: Thin film (boundary) lubrication
subtopics.theory_md:
When load is high, speed low (start-stop) or oil too thin, a full film cannot form and the asperities nearly touch. A layer only **a few molecules thick** is held on each metal surface by **physical or chemical adsorption**. Long-chain polar molecules (fatty acids, esters) stand with the polar head on the metal and the tail outward; the two layers slide over each other and stop welding.

The key property is **oiliness**, not viscosity. $\mu \approx 0.05$-$0.15$.
Lubricants: vegetable and animal oils, fatty acids, soaps, graphite, $\mathrm{MoS_2}$.
Examples: gears, cams, rail wheels, slideways.
subtopics.basics_md: Imagine two carpets facing each other: the fibres of one slide over the fibres of the other, so the floors beneath never rub. The oil molecules standing on the metal are the carpet fibres.
key_points: Occurs at high load, low speed, start-stop or thin oil
Film a few molecules thick, held by adsorption
Oiliness is the deciding property
Lubricants: vegetable/animal oils, fatty acids, graphite, $\mathrm{MoS_2}$; gears, cams

subtopics.title: Extreme pressure lubrication
subtopics.theory_md:
At **very high load and speed** the contact temperature is so high that even a boundary film desorbs or the oil decomposes, and the metals would weld.

**EP additives:** chlorinated esters, sulphurised oils, tricresyl phosphate. At the hot spots they **react chemically with the metal**, forming a film of metal chloride, sulphide or phosphide:
$\mathrm{Fe + S \rightarrow FeS}$, $\mathrm{Fe + Cl_2 \rightarrow FeCl_2}$, $\mathrm{FePO_4}$.

The film has a **high melting point and low shear strength**: it survives the heat, shears easily and prevents welding. Used in hypoid gears, rolling mills, heavy cutting.
subtopics.basics_md: If a wax coating melts off a hot pan, a new coating baked on the metal itself keeps working. EP additives bake a protective layer onto the metal when it is hottest.
key_points: For very high load, speed and temperature

subtopics.title: Classification of liquid lubricants
subtopics.theory_md:
Lubricants are classed by state: liquid, semi-solid, solid. **Liquid lubricants (oils)** are of four kinds:
1. **Animal and vegetable oils:** tallow, lard, whale, neatsfoot; castor, palm, olive, coconut, rapeseed. Good oiliness; oxidise, gum, costly.
2. **Mineral (petroleum) oils:** paraffinic and naphthenic fractions of crude. Cheap, stable; poor oiliness.
3. **Blended oils:** mineral oil plus additives: oiliness agents (castor oil), VI improvers (polyisobutylene), pour-point depressants, antioxidants, EP agents. E.g. multigrade engine oils.
4. **Synthetic oils:** silicones, polyglycols, esters, PAO.
subtopics.basics_md: Natural oils are good at sticking to metal but spoil in air. Mineral oils are tough and cheap but slippery in the wrong way. Blending takes the best of both.

subtopics.title: Vegetable and animal oils versus mineral oils
subtopics.theory_md:
Vegetable and animal oils are **triglycerides**: esters of glycerol with long-chain fatty acids (palmitic, stearic, oleic, ricinoleic). The polar ester group adsorbs on metal, giving **high oiliness**; they are **biodegradable and non-toxic**.

Disadvantages: the C=C bonds make them **oxidise** to gum and rancid acids; they **hydrolyse** in moisture to free fatty acids that corrode; costly; poor low-temperature behaviour. Mineral oils are saturated hydrocarbons: stable and cheap but poor in oiliness.

Hence natural oils are now used only as **oiliness (blending) agents**.
subtopics.basics_md: Cooking oil left open goes rancid and sticky. The same thing would happen inside a hot machine, which is why natural oils are used only in small amounts as additives.
key_points: Constituents: triglycerides (glycerol + fatty acids)
Advantage: high oiliness, biodegradable, non-toxic, renewable

subtopics.title: Semi-solid lubricants: greases
subtopics.theory_md:
**Grease** = lubricating oil thickened with a **metallic soap** (fillers: graphite, talc).
- **Calcium (cup) grease:** water-resistant, below about 80 °C.
- **Sodium grease:** up to about 175 °C, not water-resistant.
- **Lithium grease:** water-resistant, wide temperature range.

**Used instead of oil** at slow speed and heavy load, intermittent working, where dust or moisture must be sealed out, where oil must not drip, and in inaccessible bearings. Higher friction and poor cooling.

**Consistency:** hardness, by cone penetration (25 °C, 5 s, tenths of mm). **Drop point:** temperature at which the first drop falls (Ubbelohde); upper temperature limit.

subtopics.title: Solid lubricants: graphite and MoS2
subtopics.theory_md:
**Solid lubricants** have a layered structure and are used where oil fails: very high load or temperature, or where oil contamination is not allowed (food, textile).

**Graphite:** each C is $sp^2$, in flat hexagonal layers (C-C 1.42 Å) about 3.35 Å apart, held by **weak van der Waals forces**, so layers slide. Used as powder, **oildag** (in oil) or **aquadag** (in water).

**$\mathrm{MoS_2}$:** sandwich layers S-Mo-S; adjacent sandwiches held by weak van der Waals forces between S layers. Works in **vacuum** and to higher temperature.

Others: talc, mica, soapstone, PTFE.
subtopics.basics_md: A deck of cards: each card is rigid, but the deck slides because cards only touch loosely. Graphite and MoS2 are decks of atom-thin cards.

Used at high load/temperature or where oil contamination is unacceptable

topics.topic: Physical and chemical properties of lubricants and their testing

subtopics.title: Viscosity and viscosity index
subtopics.theory_md:
**Viscosity** is resistance to flow, measured by the **Redwood** viscometer (No. 1 thin oils, No. 2 viscous oils) or Saybolt, as seconds for 50 mL. Too low: film breaks, wear; too high: power loss and heat. It falls as temperature rises.

**Viscosity index (VI)** is the rate of change of viscosity with temperature; **high VI = small change**. Dean and Davis scale: Pennsylvanian (paraffinic) oil = 100, Gulf coast (naphthenic) oil = 0.
$$\mathrm{VI} = \frac{L-U}{L-H}\times 100$$
$L$, $H$, $U$: viscosities at $100\,^\circ$F of the VI 0 oil, VI 100 oil and test oil; all three equal at $210\,^\circ$F. Multigrade oils (VI improvers) have high VI. IC engines need high VI.

subtopics.title: Flash point and fire point
subtopics.theory_md:
**Flash point:** lowest temperature at which the oil gives enough vapour to **ignite momentarily** when a small flame is brought near.
**Fire point:** lowest temperature at which the vapours **burn continuously for at least 5 s**. It is 5-40 °C above the flash point.

**Significance:** both must be well above the working temperature to avoid fire; a low flash point also shows volatile fractions.

**Pensky-Martens (closed cup):** oil cup with lid, shutter, pilot flame, stirrer, thermometer, air bath. Heat at 5-6 °C per minute with stirring; every 1-2 °C dip the flame into the vapour space; the first distinct flash is the flash point. Continue heating to find the fire point. Open cup alternative: Cleveland.
subtopics.basics_md: Petrol gives off vapour at room temperature and flashes easily; diesel needs warming first. A lubricant must not flash anywhere near the heat of the machine it is protecting.
key_points: Flash point: vapour ignites momentarily with flame
Fire point: burns continuously at least 5 s; 5-40 °C above flash point
Both should exceed working temperature

subtopics.title: Cloud point, pour point and aniline point
subtopics.theory_md:
**Cloud point:** temperature at which oil turns cloudy on cooling as wax separates. **Pour point:** temperature at which oil just stops flowing. Cloud point is above pour point. Low values are needed in cold climates, refrigeration and aircraft; pour-point depressants (polymethacrylates) are added.

**Test:** oil in a flat-bottom tube with thermometer, in a jacket in an ice-salt bath. Cloud point: examine at each 1 °C fall. Pour point: tilt every 3 °C; no movement in 5 s means stop; report 3 °C above.

**Aniline point:** lowest temperature at which equal volumes of oil and aniline are completely miscible. **High aniline point = few aromatics = less attack on rubber seals.**
subtopics.basics_md: Butter in a fridge clouds and then stops spreading. Cloud point is when the first haze of wax appears; pour point is when it will no longer run.
key_points: Cloud point: wax haze on cooling; pour point: oil ceases to flow

subtopics.title: Acid, saponification and other chemical values
subtopics.theory_md:
- **Acid value:** mg KOH to neutralise the free acids in 1 g oil; $=\dfrac{V\times N\times 56}{W}$. Should be **below 0.1**: free acids corrode metal and catalyse oxidation to gum.
- **Saponification value:** mg KOH to saponify 1 g oil; $=\dfrac{(B-S)\times N\times 56}{W}$ ($B$ blank, $S$ sample titre). Vegetable/animal oils saponify, mineral oils do not, so it detects fatty oil in a blend.
- **Carbon residue** (Conradson): % carbon left on heating in limited air; **low** to avoid deposits in engines.
- **Sligh oxidation number:** sludge formed on oxidation; **low** is good.
- **Iodine value:** unsaturation; high = poor oxidation stability.
subtopics.basics_md: Each number answers one worry: is the oil acidic, is it natural or mineral, does it leave soot, does it turn to sludge. Learn the worry and the right direction (low or high).

subtopics.title: Steam emulsion number (demulsibility)
subtopics.theory_md:
**Steam emulsion number (SEN):** the time in **seconds** for an oil-water emulsion, made by passing steam through the oil, to separate into two layers.

**Test:** 20 mL of oil in a standard tube is heated by steam bubbling until about 90 °C; the tube is held at about 90 °C and the time for complete separation is noted.

**Low SEN is needed** (good demulsibility) for steam turbines and marine engines, where oil meets water or steam. A stable emulsion lubricates poorly, traps dirt, forms sludge and corrodes. Refined oils have low SEN; oxidised or impure oils have high SEN. (For cutting fluids a stable emulsion is wanted.)
subtopics.basics_md: Oil and vinegar in a salad dressing separate quickly if you leave them: that is low SEN. A lubricant must do the same with water, so that the water can be drained.
key_points: SEN = time (s) for oil-water emulsion to separate
Steam bubbled into 20 mL oil to about 90 °C, time noted
Low SEN = good demulsibility
Needed for steam turbines, marine engines
Emulsion: poor lubrication, sludge, corrosion

subtopics.title: Lubricating emulsions
subtopics.theory_md:
An **emulsion** is a dispersion of one liquid as fine droplets in another immiscible liquid, stabilised by an **emulsifier** (soap, sulphonated oil). In lubrication: oil and water.
- **Oil-in-water (O/W):** oil droplets in water. Water cools, oil lubricates. Examples: cutting fluids (soluble oil), rolling oils for cold rolling.
- **Water-in-oil (W/O):** oil is the continuous phase, better lubrication, water reduces flammability. Examples: fire-resistant hydraulic fluids (coal mines, steel mills), steam-cylinder and marine lubrication.

They combine the cooling power of water with the lubricating power of oil.
subtopics.basics_md: Milk is oil droplets in water. A soluble-oil emulsion is the same idea: a milky liquid that cools like water and lubricates like oil.
key_points: Emulsion = oil + water + emulsifier
O/W: cooling, cutting fluids, rolling oils
W/O: better lubrication, fire-resistant hydraulic fluids
Combines cooling of water with lubrication of oil

subtopics.title: Cutting fluids
subtopics.theory_md:
**Cutting fluids** are applied at the tool-workpiece interface in machining. The commonest is **soluble oil**: mineral oil plus emulsifier, diluted with water to a milky O/W emulsion. For heavy cuts (threading, broaching) use **straight cutting oils**: mineral oil with fatty oil and sulphur or chlorine EP additives.

**Advantages:**
1. **Cools** tool and work: longer tool life, accurate dimensions
2. **Lubricates** tool-chip interface, less power
3. Prevents **chip welding** (built-up edge)
4. **Washes away chips**
5. Better **surface finish**; protects against corrosion

Good cutting fluid: high specific heat, non-corrosive, non-toxic, stable, non-foaming.
subtopics.basics_md: A drill bit going into steel gets red hot. A stream of milky coolant keeps it cool and slippery so that the bit lasts and the hole is smooth.
key_points: Cutting fluid = coolant and lubricant at the tool tip
Soluble oil (O/W emulsion) for general machining
Straight oils with EP additives for heavy cuts
Advantages: cooling, lubrication, no chip welding, flushing chips, finish, corrosion protection

topics.topic: Selection of lubricants for light and heavy machinery

subtopics.title: Characteristics of a good lubricant
subtopics.theory_md:
Selection depends on load, speed, temperature and environment. A good lubricant has:
1. Adequate **viscosity** and **high VI**
2. High **oiliness**
3. High **flash and fire points**
4. Low **cloud and pour points**
5. High **oxidation stability** (low Sligh number, low carbon residue)
6. Low **acid value** and low **SEN**
7. High **aniline point**, low volatility

Water is unsuitable: very low viscosity, causes corrosion, boils at 100 °C and freezes at 0 °C, and has no oiliness.
subtopics.basics_md: Choosing a lubricant is like choosing shoes: you check the terrain (load and speed), the weather (temperature) and what it will touch (rubber, water, steam).
key_points: Selection factors: load, speed, temperature, environment
Properties: viscosity, high VI, oiliness, flash point, low pour point
Oxidation stability, low acid value, low SEN, high aniline point
Water unsuitable: low viscosity, corrosion, narrow liquid range, no oiliness

subtopics.title: Light and heavy machinery
subtopics.theory_md:
**Light machinery and instruments** (watches, clocks, sewing machines, scientific instruments): low load, moderate speed. Use **low-viscosity** refined mineral oil with high oiliness and no gumming (clock oil, neatsfoot oil, light mineral oil with a little fatty oil).

**Heavy machinery** (rolling mills, crushers, cranes, heavy gears): high load, low speed, so boundary or EP conditions. Use **high-viscosity oils**, **greases**, oils with **EP additives**, or **graphite or MoS$_2$** at very high temperature.

Match viscosity to load: heavy grease in a watch jams it; thin oil in a rolling mill is squeezed out.
subtopics.basics_md: Thin oil for a delicate hinge, thick grease for a truck axle: viscosity follows the load.
key_points: Light machinery: low viscosity, oiliness, non-gumming
Heavy machinery: high viscosity oil, grease, EP additives, solid lubricants
Match viscosity to load and speed

questions.q: Suggest lubricants, with reasons, for (a) delicate instruments and (b) heavy machinery such as rolling mills.
questions.model_answer_md:
**(a) Delicate instruments:** light mineral oil or clock oil, blended with a little fatty oil. Reason: small load, so thin film is enough; oiliness for small bearings; must not gum or evaporate.

**(b) Heavy machinery:** high-viscosity oil, grease, or oil with EP additives; graphite or $\mathrm{MoS_2}$ at very high temperature. Reason: high load and low speed break thin films; EP or solid lubricants prevent welding.

subtopics.title: IC engines, turbines, transformers and refrigerators
subtopics.theory_md:
- **IC engine:** high VI, high flash point, low pour point, low carbon residue, with detergent and antioxidant additives (multigrade oil).
- **Steam turbine:** low viscosity, high oxidation stability and **low SEN** (good demulsibility), because the oil meets steam.
- **Transformer:** refined mineral oil with high dielectric strength, free of moisture, low pour point.
- **Refrigerator:** low cloud and pour point, so it flows and wax does not separate in the cold.
- **Food/textile machinery:** solid or food-grade lubricants that do not stain.
subtopics.basics_md: Each machine has one condition that matters most: heat cycle for the engine, steam for the turbine, electricity for the transformer, cold for the refrigerator.
key_points: IC engine: high VI, high flash point, low carbon residue, low pour point
Steam turbine: low SEN, oxidation stability
Transformer: high dielectric strength, no moisture
Refrigerator: low cloud and pour point

**Steam turbine oil:** the oil meets steam and water; a high SEN gives a stable emulsion that lubricates poorly and forms sludge. Low SEN means water separates quickly and can be drained.
